intro: You have arrived at Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum in Osmaniye province, a Late Hittite fortress of the 8th century BC. Why is it kept as an open-air museum? Because of a single bilingual inscription — the text that unlocked the decipherment of Luwian hieroglyphs. Let us step inside.
history: Its builders called it Azatiwataya. In the 8th century BC it was raised as the frontier fortress of the Adanawa city-state, yet the castle was abandoned shortly after its foundation. For centuries it lay silent. Then came the excavations of 1946, and with them a new life: Karatepe became Turkey's first open-air museum.
structure-1: You are now at the North Gate, the entrance on the north side of the city. Pause here for a moment and imagine arriving as a traveller long ago, passing through this opening into the fortress.
structure-2: And here is the South Gate, the entrance on the south side of the city. Like its northern twin, it was a threshold between the world outside and the life within the walls.
structure-3: Look closely at this relief: the Storm God of Karatepe. It depicts the Hittite storm god, carved in stone and still watching over the fortress where it was set.
structure-4: Now the Lion Statues. Lions in relief and in the round adorn the gates and walls. Look into their faces and imagine how they must have greeted, and warned, everyone who approached.
structure-5: These are the Sphinx Statues, silent guardians of the entrances. Part human, part beast, they stand where they were placed to protect the way in.
facts: Did you know? The Karatepe bilingual inscription carries the same text in Phoenician and in Hieroglyphic Luwian. Phoenician alphabet beside Luwian hieroglyphs: like a 'Rosetta Stone', it was pivotal in deciphering Anatolian hieroglyphs, the key that unlocked Luwian hieroglyphic — Anatolia's Rosetta Stone. And there is more. The reliefs in King Azatiwataş's fortress were never removed, so you see them exactly where the king set them. That is thanks to Halet Çambel, who led the excavation: she had the surroundings declared a national park, choosing to protect the works in place rather than move them to a museum.
outro: This brings our journey through Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. The king's reliefs have stood here for centuries; let them stay for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
